changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For operations owners at high-stakes event and ticketing businesses: "A name, not a queue. You get a named solutions engineer and account lead, a shared channel, and someone who picks up on on-sale morning." Name the people in the first meeting, not in a later support-plan walkthrough.
changes.why: The COO dismissed our tiered support plans as "a queue with a faster timer" and chose the vendor that brought named people and on-call cover for every major on-sale, so this support message lost the deal.

changes.change: Add an 'On-sale morning plan' proof asset for ticketing and event buyers: a one-page, on-paper runbook of what we do before, during and after a major on-sale, with who is on call, the shared channel, and what happens at minute four if payments start failing. Lead with "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down."
changes.why: The decider explicitly asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning, and we had nothing. The trigger was the incumbent's silence during an outage four minutes into an on-sale, so this was a missing asset, not a missing capability.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For high-stakes event and ticketing buyers, replace generic logos with a named ticketing reference customer who will speak to the buyer and say who picked up when it mattered. Marketing needs to source this reference before the line can be used.
changes.why: The rep had logos where the buyer wanted a person ("Someone who picks up"), so proof for this segment has to be a human reference, not a logo wall.

changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
changes.change: Stop leading with developer, sandbox and load-test proof for COO and operations-owner buyers. Keep it on the CTO track and open the operations conversation with the outage moment: who answers when payments fail mid on-sale.
changes.why: The sandbox load test won the CTO, but the COO who made the call in one meeting reacted only with "good." She said she buys what happens when it's down, not uptime, and after the competitor's meeting her questions shifted from throughput to names.
